entry: Intergovernmental forum of 19 countries, the European Union and the African Union. It addresses major issues of the global economy, including international financial stability, [[Climate change|climate change]] mitigation and [[Sustainable development|sustainable development]], through annual meetings of [[Head of government|heads of state and heads of government]]. Its 19 member states account for around 85% of gross world product, 75% of international trade and 56% of the global population. It was founded in 1999 in response to several world economic crises, after being foreshadowed at a June 1999 [[G7]] summit in Cologne. Since 2008 it has convened at least once a year, and in 2009 it declared itself the primary venue for international economic and financial cooperation. The African Union joined as the 21st member at the 2023 summit in India. Critics cite its limited membership, lack of enforcement powers and alleged undermining of existing international institutions.

Intergovernmental political and economic forum of seven major advanced economies: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. The [[European Union]] is a non-enumerated member. Originating from an ad hoc gathering of finance ministers in 1973, it became a formal venue for coordinating solutions to global issues such as [[Trade|trade]], security and [[Climate change|climate change]]. It has no treaty basis and no permanent secretariat. [[Russia]] was a member from 1997 until its expulsion in 2014. Observers criticize its membership as outdated and narrow.

Standard warning symbols of the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS), a [[United Nations]] framework. Two sets exist: one for container labels and workplace warnings, and one for transporting dangerous goods. Both use the same symbols for the same hazards, though transport versions come in more colors and may carry extra information. Non-transport pictograms are black symbols on a white background within a red-bordered diamond. They cover physical, health and environmental hazards, from flammability to [[Carcinogen|carcinogenicity]].

Bitmap image format developed at CompuServe and released on June 15, 1987. It holds up to 256 colors chosen from a 24-bit RGB palette, which suits logos and solid-color graphics better than photographs. A file can hold several frames for [[Animation|animation]], and the data is compressed with the lossless Lempel–Ziv–Welch (LZW) method. The 1989 enhancement, version 89a, added animation delays and transparent backgrounds. Once common on the [[World Wide Web]], GIF declined in favor of [[PNG]] for still images and MP4 for video, though short video clips are still sometimes called GIFs.

Russian foreign military intelligence agency of the General Staff of the Armed Forces. Its director reports to the Minister of Defence and the Chief of the General Staff, not directly to the president as the heads of Russia's other intelligence services do. It is reputedly Russia's largest foreign intelligence agency and maintains its own special forces units. Its roots reach back to 1810, during the [[Napoleonic Wars]], and a 1918 Soviet order established its first predecessor, a military [[Human intelligence|human intelligence]] service of the [[Red Army]].

English mathematician known for work in [[Number theory|number theory]] and [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]]. In [[Biology|biology]] he is known for the Hardy–Weinberg principle, a basic principle of population genetics. He was elected to a prize fellowship at Trinity College, [[Cambridge]], and later became a lecturer in mathematics there. Starting in 1914 he mentored [[Srinivasa Ramanujan|Ramanujan]], whose brilliance he recognized almost immediately, and the two became close collaborators. Asked by Paul Erdős what his greatest contribution to mathematics was, Hardy replied that it was the discovery of Ramanujan. His 1940 essay *A Mathematician's Apology*, written for the layperson, is often considered one of the best insights into the mind of a working mathematician.

Neolithic archaeological site in modern-day [[Turkey]], in [[Mesopotamia|Upper Mesopotamia]]. Its name means Potbelly Hill in Turkish. The settlement was occupied from around 9500 BC to at least 8000 BC, during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. Its large circular structures contain stone pillars, among the world's oldest known [[Megalith|megaliths]], many carved with animals and human figures. Their purpose is not definitively known, though the carvings offer insights into [[Prehistoric religion|prehistoric religion]]. Findings published in 2019 suggest a settlement with domestic structures and cereal processing, challenging an earlier view of the site as a sanctuary for nomads. Prehistorians disagree on whether farming led to settlement or the reverse, a debate in which the site plays a prominent role. German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began excavations in 1995. The site was designated a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 2018, and around 10% had been excavated as of 2021.

Two theorems of [[Mathematical logic|mathematical logic]] on the limits of provability in formal axiomatic systems, published by [[Kurt Gödel]] in 1931. The first states that no consistent system of axioms whose theorems can be listed by an algorithm can prove all truths about the arithmetic of natural numbers; for any such system, some true statements are unprovable within it. The second shows that no such system can demonstrate its own consistency. The theorems are interpreted as showing that [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]]'s program to find a complete and consistent set of axioms for all of mathematics is impossible. Later results, including Turing's proof that no algorithm solves the [[Halting problem|halting problem]], extended these limitations. The theorems also shaped the philosophy of mathematics and computer science.

[[Turkic peoples|Turkic]] people of medieval Inner Asia, also known as Türks, Celestial Turks or Blue Turks. Under Bumin Qaghan and his sons, they succeeded the Rouran Khaganate as the main power in the region and established the First Turkic Khaganate. By the late 6th century it stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea. The Göktürks practiced [[Tengri|Tengriism]] and left the earliest extant Turkic writing, the Orkhon inscriptions, in the Old Turkic script. The khaganate split into eastern and western branches around 581 and collapsed in 745 after a [[Uyghurs|Uyghur]] revolt backed by [[China|Tang China]]. The origin of the name Turk is unknown.

French actor and film producer, considered an icon of French cinema. He has appeared in over 200 films since 1967, mostly in leading roles, and won the César Award for Best Actor for *The Last Metro* (1980). He won the Best Actor award at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] for *Cyrano de Bergerac* (1990). He was granted [[Russia|Russian]] citizenship in 2013, and his support of [[Vladimir Putin]] caused controversy in France. He denied wrongdoing, but was charged with rape in December 2020 and convicted of sexual assault in a separate case in May 2025.

Hypothesized erogenous area of the front vaginal wall, also called the Gräfenberg spot after the German gynecologist Ernst Gräfenberg. It is typically reported 5–8 cm (2–3 in) up the wall, toward the urinary system, and may be part of the female prostate. Its existence as a distinct structure has not been proven, nor has the source of [[Female ejaculation|female ejaculation]]. Stimulation may lead to strong arousal and [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. The G-spot may be an extension of the [[Clitoris|clitoris]], which may be the actual cause of vaginal orgasms. Sexologists emphasize that not experiencing G-spot stimulation is normal.

Anticonvulsant medication, a derivative of the neurotransmitter GABA, sold as Neurontin among other brands. It treats [[Pain|neuropathic pain]] and partial seizures of [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]]. About 30–40% of people given it for diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia have a meaningful benefit. It acts on α2δ subunits of calcium channels rather than on GABA receptors. Sleepiness and dizziness are the most common side effects. In 2008 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a class-wide warning on suicide risk for gabapentinoids, although a later study found no outstanding difference in suicide attempt rates. It is often prescribed off-label despite limited evidence for many of those uses.

American video game developer and businessman, co-founder and president of [[Valve Corporation|Valve]]. He dropped out of [[Harvard University|Harvard]] in the early 1980s to join [[Microsoft]], where he spent 13 years and produced the first three releases of Windows. He also led a port of [[Doom (1993 video game)|Doom]] for Windows 95. In 1996 he left Microsoft with Mike Harrington to found Valve, whose first game was [[Half-Life (video game)|Half-Life]] (1998). Newell led development of [[Steam (service)|Steam]], launched in 2003, which controlled most of the market for downloaded PC games by 2011. [[Forbes]] estimated that he owned at least half of Valve as of 2025, and his estimated net worth is $11 billion.

Country on the Atlantic coast of [[Central Africa]], lying on the equator. Its capital and largest city is Libreville; other major cities include Port-Gentil and Franceville. The country was colonized by [[France]] in the late 19th century and became independent in 1960. Omar Bongo came to office in 1967 and built a dynasty that held power through a client network. The Gabonese Democratic Party, which long dominated politics, was removed in a 2023 coup. Gabon is one of Africa's wealthiest countries by per capita income, thanks in part to petroleum and foreign investment, yet large parts of its population are poor. Bantu groups make up about 95% of the population, and about 80% are [[Christianity|Christian]]. French is the official language, and 91% of people lived in urban areas as of 2024, the highest share in Africa.

Capital and largest city of Botswana, in the southeastern corner of the country within 15 km (9.3 mi) of the [[South Africa|South African]] border. It had 246,325 residents at the [[Census|2022 census]], about 10% of Botswana's population, and 534,842 in its metropolitan area. The city is named after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa and was planned as the capital in the mid-1960s, as Botswana approached independence. The capital moved there from Mafeking in 1965, and the city was renamed from Gaberones to Gaborone in 1969. It is the political and economic center of Botswana, home to its largest companies and the Botswana Stock Exchange, and the headquarters of the Southern African Development Community. Rapid growth has caused housing problems and illegal settlements.

French composer, organist, pianist and teacher. After training at the École Niedermeyer in Paris, he earned a modest living as an organist and teacher, and later became organist of the Église de la Madeleine and director of the Paris Conservatoire. He composed largely during summer retreats to the countryside. His best-known works include the Requiem, the Pavane, the nocturnes for piano, and the songs "Après un rêve" and "Clair de lune". His later works are more harmonically complex, and the *Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians* credits his innovations with influencing the teaching of [[Harmony|harmony]] for later generations. His pupils included [[Maurice Ravel]] and [[Nadia Boulanger]]. Increasing deafness troubled his last twenty years, and an unprecedented national tribute was held for him in Paris in 1922.

Colombian writer and journalist, a Nobel laureate in literature. Known affectionately as Gabo, he left law school for journalism and was openly critical of Colombian and foreign politics from early on. He is best known for novels that popularized magic realism, a style that places magical events in ordinary, realistic settings. *One Hundred Years of Solitude* (1967) has sold over fifty million copies worldwide. Many of his works are set in the fictional village of Macondo, inspired by his birthplace, Aracataca, and most explore solitude. He received the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. As of 2023, he is the most-translated Spanish-language author of the 21st century. Alongside [[Jorge Luis Borges]], he is regarded as one of the most renowned Latin American authors in history.

Archangel and messenger of God in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. He appears in the Book of Daniel explaining prophetic visions, and in the Gospel of Luke he announces to Zechariah the birth of [[John the Baptist]] and tells [[Mary, mother of Jesus|Mary]] that she will bear Jesus. Many Christian churches, including the [[Catholic Church]], revere him as a saint. Muslims believe he revealed the first verses of the [[Quran]] to Muhammad. Alongside the archangel Michael, he is described as the guardian angel of the Israelites.

Silvery-white [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth]] element with atomic number 64 and symbol Gd. It is the eighth member of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series. Jean Charles de Marignac discovered it in 1880 by detecting its oxide spectroscopically, and it is named after the mineral gadolinite, itself named for Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin. Pure gadolinium was first isolated by Félix Trombe in 1935. As little as 1% of it significantly improves the workability and high-temperature oxidation resistance of iron and chromium. Gadolinium absorbs neutrons, so it is used in shielding and in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]]. Chelated gadolinium compounds serve as contrast agents in [[Magnetic resonance imaging|magnetic resonance imaging]], because free gadolinium ions are highly toxic.

Personification of Earth in [[Greek mythology]]. Her name is a poetic form of the Greek word for earth. As mother of Uranus (Sky), she bore the [[Titans]], the Cyclopes and the Giants, and with Pontus (Sea) she bore the primordial sea gods. In [[Hesiod]]'s account, she arose from Chaos. Dissatisfied with Uranus hiding their children within her, she gave her son Cronus a sickle, with which he castrated his father. From the severed genitals in the sea came [[Aphrodite]]. Her Roman equivalent was Terra.

Measure of a two-port circuit's ability to increase the power or amplitude of a signal. It is usually the ratio of output to input signal amplitude or power, often expressed in [[Decibel|decibels]] (dB). Gain above one is amplification, the defining property of an active device such as an [[Amplifier|amplifier]]; a passive circuit has gain below one. The term alone is ambiguous: audio and operational amplifiers usually mean voltage gain, and radio-frequency amplifiers usually mean power gain. Power gain in decibels is 10 log₁₀(Pout / Pin) dB, and voltage gain is 20 log₁₀(Vout / Vin) dB when input and output impedances are equal. In [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]] design, gain instead compares a directional antenna's radiation intensity with that of a lossless antenna.

King of the [[Vandals]] and Alans (r. 428–477). He led the Vandals from Hispania to [[North Africa]] in 428/429 and seized [[Carthage]] in 439. After the murder of Roman emperor Valentinian III, whose daughter had been betrothed to Gaiseric's son Huneric, he invaded Italy and sacked Rome in June 455. He repulsed major Roman attempts to retake North Africa in 460 and 468, and he made the Vandals a major Mediterranean power. He died in Carthage in 477 and was succeeded by Huneric.

Javanese general and mahapatih (chief minister) of the [[Majapahit|Majapahit Empire]]. He is credited with unifying the Nusantara archipelago and bringing Majapahit to its peak. According to legend, he swore the *Sumpah Palapa*, vowing not to rest until the archipelago was unified. Historical accounts of his career come mainly from the *Pararaton* and the *Nagarakretagama*, a Javanese eulogy, and an inscription from the mid-14th century. He is considered an important national hero in [[Indonesia]] and a symbol of [[Patriotism|patriotism]] and national unity. His popular image derives largely from a 1945 book by Mohammad Yamin, whose depiction many people dispute.

Ecuadorian volcanic archipelago in the eastern [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]], lying around the equator about 898 km (558 mi) west of South America. It had a population of slightly over 33,450 in 2020. Its many endemic species were studied by [[Charles Darwin]] in the 1830s and inspired his theory of evolution by [[Natural selection|natural selection]]. Pirates used the islands as a base to raid Spanish shipping during the Golden Age of Piracy, and the goats and rats introduced then greatly damaged several islands' ecosystems. [[Ecuador]] formally claimed the islands in 1832, and all of them are now protected as part of Galápagos National Park and Marine Reserve. Designated a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1978, the islands face threats from invasive species and tourism.

Species of giant tortoise, *Chelonoidis niger*, the largest living tortoise, native to the [[Galápagos Islands]]. Adults can weigh up to 417 kg (919 lb), and wild individuals may live over 100 years. Shell shape varies by island: domed shells on humid highlands and saddleback shells on dry lowlands, a pattern that [[Charles Darwin]] observed in 1835 and that contributed to his theory of evolution. Numbers fell from over 250,000 in the 16th century to around 15,000 in the 1970s, through hunting for meat and oil, habitat clearance and introduced animals. Lonesome George, the last known individual of one subspecies, died in June 2012. Conservation has released captive-bred juveniles, and all surviving subspecies are classified as Threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
